topic: Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026

subtopics.title: NEET-UG 2024 leak and the 2024 Act
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Amendment follows the NEET-UG 2024 paper leak controversy, in which alleged leak networks were reported in Patna (Bihar) and Hazaribagh (Jharkhand). Investigations and Supreme Court monitoring exposed organised cheating syndicates. Parliament responded by enacting the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, which the text describes as India's first dedicated central legislation on this issue.
facts: NEET-UG 2024 paper leak: alleged leak networks in Patna (Bihar) and Hazaribagh (Jharkhand)
67 candidates secured full marks, aided by disputed grace marks
The full-marks outcome triggered nationwide protests and judicial scrutiny
CBI investigation and Supreme Court monitoring exposed organised cheating syndicates
Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 was enacted in response
The Act is India's first dedicated central legislation on paper leaks, organised cheating and exam-related fraud
Act covers exams by UPSC, SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards, National Testing Agency and Institute of Banking Personnel Selection
Later controversy intensified demands for stronger deterrence and faster legal proceedings

subtopics.title: Harsher punishments under the 2026 Amendment
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Amendment revises penalties across four categories: individual offences, service providers, organised examination crime and organised crimes. Individual offences move from 3-5 years to 5-10 years, and the service-provider ban rises from 4 years to 8 years. Organised examination crime and organised crimes also get revised minimum terms and fines.
facts: Individual offences: 3-5 years earlier, 5-10 years under the amendment
Individual offences: fine up to ₹50 lakh under the amendment
Service providers: ban raised from 4 years to 8 years
Organised examination crime: at least 3 years and ₹1 crore fine earlier
Organised examination crime: at least 5 years and ₹5 crore fine under the amendment
Organised crimes: at least 7 years and ₹10 crore fine under the amendment
The booklet table compares earlier and amended provisions for all four categories

subtopics.title: Speedy trial: Fast-Track Courts and timelines
subtopics.summary: The amendment gives statutory backing to Fast-Track Courts for offences under the Act and sets a combined timeline for investigation and trial. Appeals before High Courts are heard by a two-judge bench and disposed of within a fixed period. Supreme Court precedents treat speedy trial as a fundamental right and recognise that no fixed time limit can be set for all criminal trials.
facts: Statutory backing for Fast-Track Courts to try offences under the Act
Initial Fast-Track Courts announced in 4 High Courts where NEET-related cases are pending
11th Finance Commission (2000-2005) first recommended Fast Track Courts in 2000
Combined timeline: investigation within 2 months and trial within 3 months, 5 months in all
Appeals before High Courts heard by a 2-Judge Division Bench and disposed of within 3 months
Aim: examination fraud cases should not remain pending for prolonged periods
Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979): speedy trial recognised as a Fundamental Right under Article 21
P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of Karnataka (2002): no fixed time limit can be prescribed for concluding criminal trials
Fast-Track Special Courts set up in October 2019 under a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for rape and POCSO Act cases

subtopics.title: Special Task Force and high-powered task force
subtopics.summary: The Union Government is empowered to set up a Special Task Force for investigating offences under the Act, which is particularly relevant to inter-state paper-leak networks. The government has also constituted a high-powered task force under Nandan Nilekani's chairmanship to drive strategic policy reforms.
facts: Union Government empowered to establish a Special Task Force for investigating offences under the Act
The Special Task Force is particularly relevant to inter-state paper-leak networks and organised criminal syndicates
High-powered Task Force constituted under Nandan Nilekani's chairmanship
Nandan Nilekani is Co-Founder of Infosys
Nandan Nilekani is Founding Chairman of the Unique Identification Authority of India
Mandate of the task force: drive strategic policy reforms

quizzes.passage: The NEET-UG 2024 controversy drew national attention after a paper leak was alleged in the examination. Alleged leak networks were reported in Patna and Hazaribagh, and the case showed how a question paper could be compromised before the test was held. Both places were linked to these alleged networks. Candidates in the examination were affected, and the controversy drew attention across the country. A group of candidates secured full marks, and the way those results were produced became a key point of dispute. Investigations later exposed organised cheating syndicates that had worked to compromise the examination process. Monitoring by the Supreme Court kept the case under close watch while the investigations continued. In response, Parliament passed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act in 2024. The Act applies to major public examinations, including tests held by national-level recruitment and testing bodies. It is meant to deal with paper leaks, organised cheating and other forms of fraud connected with examinations. The law was therefore passed after the controversy had exposed these problems. The Act was thus a legal answer to the problems that the NEET-UG case had revealed. Its title shows that its focus is on unfair means in public examinations.

quizzes.passage: The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 followed a controversy over the NEET-UG 2024 examination, in which alleged paper leaks were reported in Patna and Hazaribagh. A group of candidates secured full marks in the same examination, and the outcome led to protests across the country. Investigations and monitoring by the Supreme Court followed. The Act is described as India's first dedicated central legislation on paper leaks, organised cheating and exam-related fraud. The Act covers major public examinations, including those conducted by UPSC and SSC. It includes a provision for a Special Task Force that can be set up to investigate offences under the law. Such a force is meant for specialised investigation and is linked to the Act's enforcement. The government has also constituted a high-powered task force to look into examination matters at a broader level. The high-powered task force is a separate body from the Special Task Force. The 2026 amendment, which Parliament has passed, adds further provisions to the framework created by the 2024 Act. The controversy that preceded the Act was widely followed, and the new provisions respond to demands for faster legal proceedings. Alleged leaks were the subject of investigation, and the NEET-UG case remained a reference point for the debate on examination fraud.
